label: Person
name: Henry Percy, 3rd Earl of Northumberland
summary:
Henry Percy, 3rd Earl of Northumberland (d. 1461), was a pivotal figure in the early, tumultuous years of the Wars of the Roses, serving as a staunch and uncompromising Lancastrian commander. Inheriting the ancient earldom and its vast northern estates in 1455, Percy became a central pillar of King Henry VI's regime, his influence stretching across Northumberland, Yorkshire, and the Scottish Marches. His life and death epitomized the fierce aristocratic loyalties and devastating personal costs of England's dynastic conflict, particularly in the escalating feud with the rival House of Neville.

Percy's military career was marked by unwavering commitment to the red rose. He played a crucial role in the Lancastrian victory at the Battle of Wakefield in December 1460, where Richard, 3rd Duke of York, was killed, a significant although temporary reversal for the Yorkist cause. He subsequently led Lancastrian forces at the Second Battle of St Albans in February 1461, contributing to another decisive win that briefly restored Henry VI to his queen, Margaret of Anjou. His command of the northern levies was indispensable to the Lancastrians, forming the backbone of their field armies in the initial phase of the war.

However, Percy's unyielding loyalty ultimately led to his demise and a temporary eclipse of his family's power. He fell fighting for the Lancastrian cause at the Battle of Towton on April 7, 1461, one of the largest and bloodiest battles ever fought on English soil, which resulted in a catastrophic defeat for the Lancastrians and the ascent of Edward IV to the throne. His death, alongside many other northern lords, decimated the Lancastrian leadership and enabled Edward IV to consolidate his power, temporarily stripping the Percies of their titles and lands, which were then granted to the Nevilles.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry Percy's unwavering loyalty and death at Towton significantly impacted the immediate outcome of the Wars of the Roses, solidifying Yorkist control and temporarily altering the balance of power in northern England, although the Percy family's influence eventually recovered.

texts.title: Wikipedia: Henry Percy, 3rd Earl of Northumberland

causes: The deep-seated feud between the Houses of Percy and Neville for political dominance in northern England provided a critical catalyst for his military actions.
His inheritance of the Earldom of Northumberland in 1455 placed upon him the traditional responsibilities of leading and defending his family's extensive northern interests.
The outbreak of the Wars of the Roses in 1455 compelled powerful English magnates like Percy to align with either the Lancastrian or Yorkist factions.
effects: His death at the Battle of Towton in 1461 significantly weakened the Lancastrian cause and led to the temporary forfeiture of the Percy estates and titles.
The temporary eclipse of Percy power in the north allowed the House of Neville, particularly Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, to consolidate greater influence.
The eventual restoration of his son, Henry Percy, as 4th Earl of Northumberland, by Edward IV in 1470 demonstrated the pragmatic need for the crown to appease regional magnates.

relationships.context: Henry Percy was a leading Lancastrian commander throughout the early phase of the Wars of the Roses, fighting for King Henry VI.
Percy served as a loyal military commander and political ally to Queen Margaret of Anjou, leading Lancastrian forces in several key battles.
The fierce and long-standing rivalry between the Percy and Neville families, particularly with Richard Neville, shaped much of Henry Percy's political and military actions.
Henry Percy was killed leading the Lancastrian vanguard at the decisive Battle of Towton on April 7, 1461.
His death in battle as a Lancastrian resulted in the immediate forfeiture of the Percy earldom and vast estates to the victorious Yorkist crown.
